judged.rationale: Probability, Bayesian estimation, and statistical inference are the foundation every data scientist builds models on, even though none is distinctive to the role.
MIT's own ML sequence (6.3900, 6.C011) lists 6.3700 as a prerequisite; probability foundations are explicitly in the ML engineer skill pool.
Designing visualizations and communicating insights from real-world datasets is the analyst's dashboard-and-reporting core.
Data visualization and presenting findings from big data are named data-scientist responsibilities, even if not distinctive to the role.
An intro data-science course in Python covering statistical and simulation modeling is a standard first step toward data science.
Framing tasks as ML problems and interpreting results with robustness/fairness analysis is modeling work data scientists do daily.
Estimation, regression, and causal inference with applied data assignments are the statistical base of data-science work.
Regression and applied data analysis on real datasets support the analyst's experiment-support and metric-analysis work.
Randomized-experiment analysis, IV, and diff-in-diff are exactly the causal-inference toolkit tech data scientists use for experimentation.
Advanced causal methods plus ML applications in econometrics map onto the data scientist's modeling and experiment-analysis scope.
Data-driven decision-making in high-dimensional settings with Bayesian methods in R/Python is core industry data-science practice.
Building reliable ML solutions for decision support on high-impact applied problems is data-science work as much as ML engineering.
Designing business experiments and reading causal effects is the analyst's A/B-testing and experiment-support skill, a distinctive analyst skill in this dataset.
Applied probability, hypothesis testing, and regression are the statistical foundation data-science modeling assumes.
Probability and simulation are the mathematical base of OR modeling; the course explicitly introduces simulation.
Time series forecasting, ML for operations, and multi-armed bandits are standard data-science techniques applied to business decisions.
Prescriptive optimization applied to logistics, marketing, and finance rounds out the data scientist's modeling toolkit; the course itself cites ML and statistics applications.
Causal inference with real data in Python/R, contrasted with ML, is core experimentation work on industry data-science teams.
Optimization theory and algorithm design (including optimization under uncertainty) underpin how ML models are trained and tuned.
Using R to simulate, analyze, and visualize data plus regression and hypothesis testing supports the analyst's day-to-day analysis work.
Eigenvalues, SVD, and least squares are the mathematics behind PCA, regression, and dimensionality reduction in data-science practice.
Matrix methods and linear algebra software are the working substrate of linear programming and network models in OR.
Probability theory through standard distributions and limit theorems is the foundation of statistical modeling for data science.
